claims.text: Overall tribo-corrosion degradation in high-entropy alloys is governed by the balance between mechanical removal of a passive oxide film and its repassivation.
Mechanical sliding removes the protective passive oxide film.
Film removal faster than repassivation causes a synergistic increase in wear and corrosion.
The initial HEA has a stable passive oxide layer.
The passive oxide layer provides corrosion resistance.
The passive oxide layer provides wear resistance.
Electrolyte additives or oxygen-level adjustments can systematically modify repassivation kinetics.
Loss of the passive film exposes a surface that is more vulnerable to corrosion.
Slower repassivation will produce a higher total degradation rate than the standard-electrolyte baseline.
Slower repassivation will increase the wear contribution, observable as deeper wear tracks.
Slower repassivation will increase the corrosion contribution, observable as higher corrosion current density.
Accelerated repassivation will reduce total degradation relative to the baseline.
The prediction is intended to apply under controlled mechanical loading when repassivation kinetics are the primary varied factor.
The prediction may fail when phase transformations dominate degradation.
The prediction may fail when extensive oxidation beyond the passive film dominates degradation.
Microstructural factors may alter the quantitative effect of changing repassivation kinetics.
Modulating repassivation kinetics without changing other corrosion parameters is experimentally challenging.
A controlled comparison uses otherwise identical HEA samples under constant sliding speed and load with slowed, accelerated, and standard repassivation conditions.
Failure of repassivation changes to produce significant and directionally predictable changes in wear, corrosion, or passive-film characteristics would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
